title: VB8-05439
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I allow this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Venezuela. The Appellant submits that she would face a serious risk of persecution in Venezuela based on her political opinion. She submits that she is a member of the political opposition to the ruling regime in Venezuela. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant was not credible with respect to some of her claims and that she did not have a profile as a political activist that would expose her to a serious risk of persecution.

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution and that the RPD breached procedural fairness. The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division is whether the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant has not adduced sufficient credible evidence to establish that she would face a serious possibility in Venezuela based on her political opinion.

I find that the RPD erred. I find that the Appellant would face a serious risk of persecution in Venezuela. I base my decision on the evidence before me including new objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) that was not before the RPD.
The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention1 refugee.
I find that the RPD did not breach procedural fairness for the reasons that follow.

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD committed a breach of procedural fairness in applying an RPD Practice Notice titled Notice to parties and counsel appearing before the Refugee Protection Division - voluminous country conditions evidence dated May 7, 2018 with an effective date of June 1, 2018.

The Appellant makes three allegations on appeal: 1. That the Practice Notice is ultra vires; 2. That the RPD erred in applying the Practice Notice; and, 3. That the RPD used "specialized knowledge". The Practice Notice is not ultra vires

The justification and authority for the Practice Notice are set out in the note itself:2 The RPD has the obligation to proceed quickly and informally,3 and must provide parties a reasonable opportunity to present evidence.4 The RPD Rules require that documents a party wishes to use at a hearing be paginated and accompanied by a list5 and must be relevant.6 Some of these rules are reiterated in Chairperson's Guideline 7.7
I find that the Practice Notice conforms to the law and with the RPD's obligation and mandate to manage its own proceedings. The RPD did not err in applying the Practice Notice
The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in applying the Practice Notice to evidence adduced at the RPD hearing on June 1, 2018.

I find that the RPD did not err. The Practice Notice was issued on May 7, 2018 to take effect on June 1, 2018. The RPD provided reasonable notice that the new procedures would take effect on June 1, 2018.

Counsel had opportunity to set out a detailed rationale for additional documents both at the RPD and in post-hearing submissions. Counsel did not do so. The RPD did not err in applying "specialized knowledge"

The Appellant argues on appeal that when the RPD interpreted and applied the Practice Notice at the RPD hearing, the RPD used its knowledge of the past practice on the part of the Appellant's Counsel with respect to submitting evidence to the RPD. The Appellant argues that in doing so, the RPD used its "specialized knowledge"8 without disclosing to the parties in advance that it intended to do so, and thereby breached natural justice.

I find that the RPD did not err. I have no evidence before me that the RPD used its knowledge of the Appellant's Counsel's past practice to alter the application of the Practice Notice or the conduct of hearing in a manner that breaches procedural fairness.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.9 As part of my analysis, I have conducted an independent assessment of the evidence and the arguments.10

When a person swears to the truth of certain allegations before the Immigration and Refugee Board, there is a presumption that those allegations are true unless there is a reason to doubt their truthfulness. This presumption of truthfulness does not apply to inferences or conclusions a witness may draw from facts, or to speculation for which there is no evidentiary basis.11

The presumption that a person's sworn testimony is true may be rebutted where problems are identified with the testimony. These problems can include contradictions, inconsistencies, and omissions; incoherent or vague testimony; limited knowledge of key elements of the case; or a reliance on false documents. The Appellant's profile is sufficient to give rise to a serious risk of persecution

The RPD found: I find that more likely than not she is being question[sic] in relation to an investigation into past corruption as noted in the documents. Although the objective evidence speaks of repeated practices of harassment and detention of demonstrators and those who disagree with the government, I find that given the evidence before this panel, that there is not sufficient reliable evidence to find that the claimant has a profile sufficient for her to face similar systemic attention from authorities.12

I find that the Appellant has submitted sufficient, credible evidence to establish that she was politically active in Venezuela. She has submitted membership cards from political parties, affidavits attesting to her involvement in Venezuelan politics, and pictures of her attendance at demonstrations. The Appellant adduced two warrants for her to appear for questioning by the Venezuelan intelligence organization Servicio Bolivariano de Inteligencia Nacional. I find that the RPD erred in finding that her profile was not sufficient to attract attention form the authorities.

The NDP for Venezuela dated September 30, 2020 contains recent information from the European Asylum Support Office (EASO) of the European Union. In a report dated August 2020, the EASO found that: FundaRedes [Human Rights Non-Governmental Organization in Venezuela] explained that high-profile activists have some degree of protection due to their visibility, but low-profile activists are more vulnerable and end up being affected even more due to their low visibility on public media, particularly at the neighbourhood level where government supporters constantly harass them.13

The Appellant also testified that she had been romantically involved with a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The EASO report states: The OVV [Observatorio Venezolano de Violencia (Venezuelan Observatory of Violence)] indicated that the risk for low-profile activists sometimes consists of the association that the activist has with high-profile ones that are more difficult to target and, as a way to 'send a message', the perpetrator act against the low-profile individual.14

Based on the evidence before me, including new NDP evidence that was not before the RPD, I find that the Appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution in Venezuela based on her political opinion. The agent of persecution is the state and groups in society allied to the ruling party in Venezuela. I find that state protection and internal flight alternatives in Venezuela are not available to the Appellant.

The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. (signed) Michael J. Gardiner Michael J.
